"He Wants Things. I Can Tell. But He Just Can't Ask."
You watch your child stare at the cookie jar on the counter. His eyes lock onto it. His body tenses. Then the cry comes — loud, desperate, unrelenting. Or maybe he grabs your hand and drags you to the kitchen, pulling you like a tool rather than talking to you like a person. You know what he wants. He knows what he wants. But the bridge between wanting and asking doesn't exist yet.
This is not a behaviour problem. This is a communication gap — and it has a name, a science, and a solution. Requesting — known clinically as manding in Applied Behaviour Analysis — is the most foundational communication skill a child can develop. When this bridge is missing, children resort to the only tools they have: crying, grabbing, tantrums, or shutting down entirely.
You are not failing. Your child's communication system is still under construction. And you are about to become its architect.

The Neuroscience of Requesting: Why Your Child Grabs Instead of Asks
Requesting is not a single skill — it is a symphony of neural processes that must fire in sequence. When any one link is underdeveloped, the requesting chain breaks, and crying, grabbing, or tantrums become the brain's backup system.
1
Motivation
Hypothalamus / Limbic System: Your child must WANT something strongly enough to act. This is the establishing operation — the internal drive state that initiates communication.
2
Intentional Communication
Prefrontal Cortex: The child must recognise that another person can fulfil this want — that communication is a tool with a purpose directed at someone else.
3
Response Selection
Broca's Area / Motor Cortex: The child must select and execute a communicative response — a word, a sign, a picture exchange, or a button press.
4
Cause-Effect Association
Basal Ganglia: The child must connect "I did this → I got that" into a repeatable, reliable loop the brain will seek out again.
The materials and techniques on this page strengthen each link in this chain — building the neural superhighway from wanting to asking.
Requesting in the Developmental Landscape
For children with autism or communication delays, the developmental timeline is shifted — but it is not cancelled. The sequence remains the same; the pace is different. A 4-year-old learning to request with pictures is following the same neurological sequence as a 12-month-old learning to point.
6–9 Months
Intentional vocalisations, reaching toward objects, gaze shifting between person and object — proto-requesting emerges.
9–12 Months
Pointing, showing, giving — early communicative gestures emerge. First "requests" are gestural.
12–18 Months
First words emerge. Early requesting via single words ("more," "up," "juice"). ← Teaching requesting directly supports this milestone.
18–24 Months
Two-word combinations for requesting ("want cookie," "more juice"). Vocabulary explosion begins in earnest.
24–36 Months
Requesting with sentences, requesting absent items, requesting information ("Where's my truck?").

This technique applies to: Children at ANY point on this timeline who have limited or no functional requesting skills (age band: 18 months – 6 years). The brain doesn't skip steps — it takes them at its own pace.
→ See the evidence grade for this intervention
Clinically Validated. Home-Applicable. Parent-Proven.
LEVEL I EVIDENCE — Systematic Reviews & Meta-Analyses
NCAEP Classification (2020)
Manding (requesting) training is classified as an evidence-based practice by the National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence and Practices, with the strongest evidence base of any verbal operant intervention.
80–90% Behaviour Reduction
Functional Communication Training (FCT) — which includes systematic manding instruction — reduces challenging behaviour by 80–90% when the communicative alternative is reinforced consistently. (Tiger, Hanley & Bruzek, 2008 — JABA)
Home-Based = Clinic-Based Outcomes
Home-based implementation of manding programmes by trained parents produces outcomes comparable to clinic-based delivery, with added generalisation advantages. (Nigam, Schlosser & Lloyd, 2006)
PECS — Level I RCT Evidence
Picture Exchange Communication System has Level I evidence from multiple randomised controlled trials demonstrating increased independent requesting in children with autism. (Flippin, Reszka & Watson, 2010)
Pinnacle Real-World Evidence
Across 80+ Pinnacle Blooms centres and 21 million+ therapy sessions, children receiving structured manding training show measurable requesting repertoire expansion within 4–8 weeks, with 97%+ of families reporting improved communication quality of life.
Teaching Requesting (Manding): What It Is
SLP-FCT-02
Ages 18 months – 6 years
Daily Practice
Formal Name: Manding Repertoire Development / Functional Communication Training — Requesting Component
Parent-Friendly Name: Teaching Your Child to Ask for What They Want

Teaching requesting is the systematic process of building your child's ability to communicate their wants and needs through any modality — speech, signs, pictures, or technology. In Applied Behaviour Analysis, a "mand" is a request that directly benefits the speaker. The MODALITY doesn't matter — the FUNCTION does. Requesting is successful when the child's signal reliably produces the desired result.
Session Duration
10–20 minutes for home sessions, with requesting opportunities embedded throughout the day in natural routines.
Frequency
Daily — minimum 20–50 requesting opportunities per day across natural routines and structured practice.
Disciplines
Speech-Language Pathology | Applied Behaviour Analysis | Special Education
→ See which therapy disciplines use this technique
A Multi-Disciplinary Approach: Who Uses This Technique
Requesting crosses every therapy discipline because communication is not a therapy category — it is the foundation of human connection. Here is how each specialist contributes.
Speech-Language Pathologist (SLP)
Primary Lead. Designs the communication system, selects the right modality (speech, signs, pictures, AAC device), builds vocabulary, and ensures the requesting repertoire expands systematically. Also addresses oral-motor foundations that support verbal requesting.
Board Certified Behaviour Analyst (BCBA)
Primary Lead. Engineers the behavioural framework — identifying motivating operations, designing prompt hierarchies, programming reinforcement schedules, and systematically fading support. Manding is the cornerstone of Verbal Behaviour programming.
Occupational Therapist (OT)
Supporting Role. Ensures sensory and motor readiness — fine motor skills for sign language, hand-over-hand guidance for picture exchange, and sensory regulation that allows the child to be in a ready state for communication.
Special Educator (SpEd)
Supporting Role. Integrates requesting into academic and pre-academic routines — requesting materials during art, requesting turns during circle time, requesting help with tasks. Drives generalisation across structured environments.
Precision Targets: What Teaching Requesting Addresses
🎯 Primary Target: Independent Requesting Repertoire
The child initiates requests for desired items, activities, actions, and information — using any communication modality — without prompting, across multiple settings and communication partners. Observable indicators: Child independently requests at least 10 different items/activities, uses requesting across 3+ settings, initiates requests with 3+ communication partners.
🔵 Secondary Targets
Reduction of challenging behaviour: When requesting works faster than crying or tantrums, challenging behaviour naturally decreases (80–90% reduction documented in FCT literature). Social initiation: Every request is a social initiation — communication directed toward another person. Cause-effect understanding: "I do this → I get that" becomes a reliable cognitive schema.
🟢 Tertiary Targets — Long-Term Developmental Gains
Expressive language foundation: Requesting vocabulary becomes the scaffold for labelling, commenting, and conversational language. Self-advocacy: The child learns "I have needs, I can communicate them, and my communication matters." Caregiver relationship quality: When communication replaces frustration, parent-child interaction transforms profoundly. Reduced caregiver dependence: The Caregiver Dependence Reduction Index shifts from need-anticipation to self-advocacy.

Essential Starter Kits: Choose Your Path
You don't need everything at once. Choose the starter path that best matches your resources and your child's current abilities. Each path has been validated across hundreds of Pinnacle Blooms families.
Path A — No Tech
Controlled access setup (free) + Core vocabulary cards + Choice boards. Best for families starting from scratch with limited resources.
Path B — Low Tech
One single-message device + Picture exchange materials + Controlled access. Ideal when your child has some imitation skills and tolerates structure.
Path C — High Tech
AAC app on an existing tablet + Controlled access + Help-required toys. Great when your child is already drawn to screens and technology.

Families who begin with just one well-chosen material and implement it consistently achieve faster early progress than families who attempt all 9 at once. Start focused. Expand as confidence grows.
Everything Else You Need (Most of It Is Already in Your Home)
Environmental Setup Materials
  • Clear storage bins or containers to store preferred items visibly
  • A designated "requesting station" — a consistent spot where materials are organised and accessible
  • Timer (phone timer works) for session structure
  • Notebook or phone for data tracking
Your Child's Reinforcer Inventory
Build a personal list of items your child is genuinely motivated by. These drive requesting:
  • Favourite snacks (broken into small portions for multiple opportunities)
  • Favourite toys (especially ones requiring help to operate)
  • Favourite activities (bubbles, tickles, swinging, songs)
  • Favourite sensory experiences (spinning, bouncing, deep pressure)

Critical Setup Principle: Every item in your reinforcer inventory should be available ONLY through requesting during structured teaching. When the child can simply take the item, there is no motivation to request.

Safety Note: Basic needs — food when hungry, water, comfort, safety — should NEVER require requesting. Controlled access applies to PREFERRED items during TEACHING sessions only, not to meeting basic human needs.
Critical Safety Protocols for Teaching Requesting
🔴 ALWAYS honour requests immediately
When your child makes a requesting attempt — no matter how imperfect — deliver the requested item IMMEDIATELY. A request that doesn't produce a result teaches the child that communication doesn't work. This is the single most critical rule.
🔴 Requesting must be faster than problem behaviour
If crying gets juice in 5 seconds but using a picture takes 30 seconds, the child will choose crying. The requesting response must be the FASTEST route to reinforcement — every single time.
🔴 Accept approximations
A child reaching toward a picture is an approximation. A sound that resembles a word is an approximation. Shape over time — don't demand perfection. Progress, not perfection, is the goal.
🔴 Never withhold basic needs
Controlled access is for PREFERRED items during TEACHING. Food when hungry, water, comfort, safety, medical needs — these are always freely available, no requesting required.
🔴 Watch for frustration build-up
If the child shows escalating distress, PROMPT the requesting response immediately and deliver the item. The goal is SUCCESS, not struggle. A successful session, even a brief one, is worth more than a long, stressful one.

When to Pause: Child is ill, tired, or in sensory overload · Child shows signs of learned helplessness · Child becomes aggressive toward materials or people · You are frustrated or exhausted — your state matters too.

Setting Up Your Home Requesting Environment
A well-prepared environment dramatically reduces friction and maximises learning. Set up takes just 5 minutes — and the difference it makes is enormous.
1
Choose a Location
Select a consistent spot — kitchen table, living room floor, or play area. Consistency helps your child understand when "requesting practice" is beginning.
2
Set Up Preferred Items
Arrange 3–5 highly preferred items in clear containers or on a high shelf — VISIBLE but not independently accessible. Seeing without reaching creates the want.
3
Place Communication Tools
PECS book or choice board on the table · Visual sign guide on the wall · AAC device charged and ready · You positioned at eye level if using speech as the modality.
4
Remove Distractions
Minimise competing reinforcers — turn off the TV, put away freely available toys. If something better is already accessible, motivation to request disappears.
5
Set Your Timer
10–15 minutes. Brief, successful sessions are always better than long, frustrating ones. End on a win — every single time.

The Environmental Sabotage Zones: Kitchen — snacks in clear containers child can't open · Playroom — favourite toy in transparent bin with lid, puzzle with 1–2 pieces held back · Bathroom — favourite bath toy visible but out of reach · Outdoors — bubbles, balls, chalk in a bag that needs opening. Every environment becomes a requesting opportunity when you control access to preferred items.

Before You Begin: The 60-Second Readiness Check
A quick check before each session prevents frustration and maximises the learning window. If any check fails, adjust first — then begin.
Check Your Child
  • Alert and regulated — not tired, hungry, ill, or in sensory overload
  • Shows interest in at least 1–2 items in the environment
  • Positioned comfortably — seated, standing, or on the floor
  • Not currently engaged in a preferred activity (you need motivation toward something NEW)
Check Yourself
  • You are calm, patient, and ready to celebrate approximations
  • You know which communication modality you're teaching today
  • You remember: HONOUR EVERY REQUEST IMMEDIATELY
  • You accept: 3 successful requests in 15 minutes = a great session
Check Your Setup
  • 3–5 preferred items visible but controlled
  • Communication tools ready (pictures / device / sign guides)
  • Timer set — 10–15 minutes
  • Data sheet or phone ready for tracking
  • Distractions minimised

If any check fails, adjust and try again later. A frustrated parent + dysregulated child = no learning. Timing is everything.
Step 1 — Create the Wanting (2–3 Minutes)
The Establishing Operation
This is NOT a test. This is an invitation to communicate. Before your child can request, they must WANT — and your job in this step is to make that want active and real.
Show, don't tell
Pick up a preferred item. Play with it yourself. Show excitement. Blow the bubbles. Spin the top. Eat one chip slowly with visible enjoyment. Let your child SEE what they're missing.
Offer a taste
Give your child a brief (3–5 second) interaction with the preferred item — one bubble, one chip, one spin of the toy. Then PAUSE. Hold the item. Wait.
Create the gap
The child has experienced the reinforcer and now it's gone. The wanting is active. This is the establishing operation — the motivational state that drives communication forward.

What NOT to do: Don't say "Use your words" — you haven't taught the HOW yet · Don't withhold for more than 5–10 seconds initially · Don't use items the child doesn't actually want — motivation must be REAL.
Step 2 — Show Them HOW to Ask (The Prompt)
The Prompt Hierarchy
Your child wants the item. The motivation is active. Now you SHOW them the requesting response. The golden rule: the MOMENT the requesting response occurs — even with full physical help — the item is delivered. No delay. No additional demands.
Picture Exchange
Physically guide child's hand to the picture → place picture in your hand → immediately give item. Say "You asked for [item]! Here you go!" Fade: full physical → partial → point → independent.
Sign Language
Mould child's hands into the sign (hand-over-hand) → immediately give item. Say the word AS the child signs: "MORE! You said more! Here's more!" Fade: full → partial → gesture model → independent.
Device / Button
Physically guide child's hand to press the button → message plays → immediately give item. Celebrate: "You asked! You pressed the button! Here it is!" Fade: full physical → partial → point → independent.
Speech
Model clearly: "COOKIE. Say cookie." → immediately give item for ANY vocal approximation. "Coo" = cookie. "Mmm" for more = more. Accept EVERYTHING initially. Fade: full model → partial → first sound cue → independent.

GOLDEN RULE: Request → Reinforcement. Every single time. No exceptions, no delays, no additional demands before the item is delivered.
Step 3 — The Requesting Loop: Want → Ask → Get → Repeat
You are now running the requesting loop — the fundamental learning cycle that builds communication. Here is what it looks like in real life with bubbles:
1
Create the Want
Blow bubbles for 5 seconds. Stop. Hold the bubble wand. Wait 3–5 seconds.
2
Catch the Signal
Child reaches, looks, vocalises, or begins to fuss → IMMEDIATELY prompt the requesting response.
3
Deliver the Reinforcer
Guide hand to "MORE" picture / mould sign / guide to button / model "more." The INSTANT the response occurs → blow more bubbles with enthusiasm: "You said MORE! More bubbles!"
4
Restart the Loop
Blow for 5–8 seconds. Stop. Hold. Wait. Run 5–8 loops per item. Switch items to maintain motivation when interest fades.

What to look for: Ideal — child begins reaching for picture/sign/button BEFORE you prompt. Acceptable — child allows prompting without resistance. Concerning — child shows no interest, actively resists, or distress escalates. If concerning: switch items, reduce demands, ensure reinforcement is immediate, and try again tomorrow.
Step 4 — Repeat, Vary, and Read Your Child (3–5 Minutes)
Target repetitions: 5–10 requesting loops per item, across 3–4 items per session = 15–40 requesting opportunities. Variety keeps motivation high and accelerates learning.
Vary the Items
Rotate through 3–4 preferred items. When interest in one fades, switch to the next to keep the establishing operation active.
Vary the Modality
For multimodal communicators: "This time, show me the picture. Now try the sign." Flexibility across modalities strengthens the communication system.
Vary the Setting
Do 5 loops at the table. Move to the floor. Try the kitchen. Requesting must work EVERYWHERE — generali­sation is built into the practice from the start.
Vary the Partner
Mum does 5 loops. Dad does 5 loops. Sibling does 5 loops. Requests must work with EVERYONE who is part of your child's life.

Reading Satiation — When to Stop: Child pushes away the item → switch or end · Response quality deteriorates → 2 more successful trials, then end on success · Child leaves the area → session is over · Timer rings → finish current loop, end on success. The Golden Ratio: 3 good requesting loops > 10 forced ones. Quality over quantity. Always.
Step 5 — Celebrate Every Request Like It's the First Word
ABA Reinforcement Principles
⚡ Timing
Reinforcement must be IMMEDIATE. Within 1–2 seconds of the requesting response. Not "in a minute." Not "after one more thing." NOW.
🎯 Specificity
Name what the child did. "You ASKED for more!" "You showed me the PICTURE!" "You SIGNED help!" — not just "Good job." Specific praise links the action to the outcome.
📣 Magnitude
Match enthusiasm to developmental level. For early learners, reinforcement should be dramatic — big smiles, excited voice, immediate delivery. As skills strengthen, natural consequences become sufficient.

Reinforcement Menu: Natural consequence (most powerful) — the requested item/activity itself · Social praise — "YES! You asked for bubbles!" · Physical celebration — high-five, tickle, hug · Token economy (for advanced learners). The requested item IS the reinforcement. You do not need to add a reward on top. The juice is the reinforcer. The praise is the bonus.

Never withhold the requested item after a correct response to "test" the child. Every request honoured. Every time.
Step 6 — End Strong, End Happy (2 Minutes)
How you close a session shapes how your child feels about the next one. Always aim to finish on a note of success, calm, and connection.
1
Final Success Loop
Ensure the last requesting loop is successful. If the child is struggling, prompt fully — the last experience should always be positive and reinforcing.
2
Free Access Period
After the session, give 2–3 minutes of free access to preferred items with no demands. This prevents the child from associating the end of practice with losing access to good things.
3
Transition Signal
"All done practising! Great asking today!" Use a visual schedule card if available to mark the transition clearly and predictably.
4
Quick Data Note
Record on phone or data sheet: number of requesting attempts · prompted vs. independent · most motivating item · any new approximations or improvements observed.
5
Self-Care Check
How are YOU feeling? Teaching communication is emotionally demanding. Acknowledge your effort. You showed up. That matters enormously — to your child and to yourself.

The One Number That Matters: Independence Ratio
Independence Ratio = Independent Requests ÷ Total Requests
Week 1
Expected — most requests will be prompted. This is completely normal and correct.
Week 3
Signals real learning. The neural pathway is forming and the child is beginning to initiate.
Week 6
The skill is consolidating. Prompts can be faded more aggressively at this stage.
Week 8+
Your child is a requester. Communication is becoming a lifestyle, not a therapy activity.
When It's Not Working: Troubleshooting Guide
Problem 1: "My child shows no interest in any items."
The establishing operation is missing. Try offering items after a period of deprivation (before snack time, not after), introducing novel items, and observing what your child gravitates toward naturally in unstructured play.
Problem 2: "My child gets frustrated and has a meltdown before requesting."
Your prompt is too late or the delay is too long. Prompt BEFORE frustration. As soon as the child shows interest → prompt the requesting response → deliver immediately. Speed is everything in early teaching.
Problem 3: "My child requests with prompting but never independently."
Prompt dependency. Implement a time delay: wait 3 seconds before prompting, then 5, then 10. Give the child TIME to initiate before stepping in. Fade systematically rather than all at once.
Problem 4: "My child only requests with me, not with others."
Generalisation gap. Systematically introduce new communication partners. Have them observe first, then practise with your support, then independently. Every new partner gets 2–3 training sessions.
Problem 5: "My child throws the communication materials."
The child may be communicating "I don't want to do this" or may be frustrated. Reduce demands. Use HIGHER preference items. Ensure the requesting response is easier than the problem behaviour.
Problem 6: "My child can label items but doesn't request them."
Common in Verbal Behaviour: the child has tacts (labels) but not mands (requests). Create motivation — withhold the labelled item and prompt the requesting form. "You said 'cookie' — you WANT cookie? Here's cookie!"

Make This Yours: Adapting the Technique to Your Child
No two children are identical. The technique framework is evidence-based; how you apply it should be tailored to your child's current abilities, sensory profile, and the rhythms of your family's day.
EASIER VERSION
For early learners or difficult days: 1–2 HIGHLY preferred items only · Accept ANY communicative attempt (reach, vocali­sation, eye gaze) · Prompt immediately — no waiting · 5 loops total. That's enough. End on success.
STANDARD VERSION
3–4 items, specific requesting response expected · 3–5 second wait before prompting · 15–40 requesting opportunities per session · Track independence ratio data consistently.
HARDER VERSION
For advancing learners: request absent items (item not visible) · sentence strips ("I want + [item]") · novel partners · novel settings · Deny occasional requests and teach "wait" / "later" calmly.
Age-Based Adaptations
18–24 months
Focus on gestures, single signs, or single-button devices. Physical prompting dominant. Accept all approximations generously.
2–3 years
Picture exchange, multi-sign vocabulary, core word cards. Begin fading prompts systematically.
3–4 years
AAC apps, sentence construction, verbal approximations. Teach requesting in group settings.
5–6 years
Multi-word requests, requesting information, requesting actions, requesting help with specific tasks.

Sensory Profile Adaptations: Sensory seekers — use high-intensity reinforcers (spinning, bouncing, loud toys). Requesting earns sensory input. Sensory avoiders — use calm reinforcers (quiet toys, preferred foods, gentle activities). Keep sessions in a regulated sensory environment.
Weeks 1–2: The Foundation Phase
What You WILL See
  • Child tolerates the requesting routine without significant resistance
  • Child allows physical prompting to produce requesting responses
  • Child begins to show anticipation when preferred items appear
  • You become more comfortable with the prompting sequence
What You Will NOT See Yet
  • Independent requesting — this is normal, prompting is expected
  • Generalisation to other settings — that comes later
  • Dramatic behaviour reduction — the neural pathways are still forming

The Real Progress Indicator: If your child participates in 3–5 requesting loops per session without significant distress — that IS progress. The child is tolerating a new communication demand. That tolerance is the foundation everything else builds on.

Parent Milestone: "By the end of Week 2, you should feel confident in the prompting sequence and be able to run a 10-minute session without referring to instructions."
Weeks 3–4: The Consolidation Phase
Child reaches for materials BEFORE you prompt
Anticipatory behaviour: your child looks at you, then at the item, then at the communication tool. The sequence is being internalised.
First independent or semi-independent requests
Even one unprompted request is profoundly significant. The neural pathway fired on its own. Note the date — this is a milestone worth recording.
Reduced latency and new partners
Faster time from wanting to requesting. The child may begin requesting with a second communication partner — generalisation is beginning to emerge.

What's happening neurologically: The neural pathway from wanting → requesting response → reinforcement is strengthening through repetition. Synaptic connections are forming. The brain is learning: "This communication thing WORKS."

When to Increase: If your child shows 30%+ independence, begin fading prompts more aggressively. Increase the time delay before prompting from 3 seconds to 5 seconds.
Weeks 5–8: The Emergence Phase
Independent requesting is becoming the norm
Requesting vocabulary expanding — new items, new signs, new pictures entering the repertoire each week.
Spontaneous requesting in non-teaching moments
"He just walked up and handed me the juice picture — at dinner!" These unprompted generalisations signal that communication is becoming a lifestyle.
Challenging behaviour decreasing
Tantrums, grabbing, and crying are reducing because requesting now WORKS faster. Your child has a better tool and is choosing to use it.
"He walked to the fridge, got his picture book, found the juice picture, and handed it to me. No prompting. No crying. Just... asking." This moment changes everything. You will know it when it happens.

What to do now: Expand vocabulary — introduce 2–3 new requesting items per week · Expand partners — ensure 3–4 people can respond · Expand settings — practice requesting in the community · Begin moving toward multi-word requests ("want + cookie" instead of just "cookie").
Every Request Is a Victory — Celebrate These Milestones
Progress in communication is not always linear, but every milestone your child reaches is evidence that the hard work is working. Record these moments — you will want to return to them on difficult days.
Milestone 1: First Prompted Request
Your child produced a requesting response with physical guidance. The loop is established. Date achieved: ___
Milestone 2: First Independent Request
Your child requested WITHOUT prompting. The neural pathway fired on its own. Date achieved: ___
Milestone 3: First Novel Request
Your child requested an item you never specifically taught. Generalisation has begun. Date achieved: ___
Milestone 4: First Multi-Partner Request
Your child requested from someone other than the primary teacher. Communication is becoming universal. Date achieved: ___
Milestone 5: First Spontaneous Request Outside Teaching
Your child requested during a natural routine without any setup. Communication is becoming a lifestyle. Date achieved: ___
Milestone 6: First Multi-Word Request
"Want juice" or "More bubbles" — combining words to refine requests. Language is growing. Date achieved: ___

📸 Photo/Journal Prompt: Take a video of your child's first independent request. You will want to watch this video on hard days. This is evidence that communication is possible.
When to Seek Additional Support
🔴 Seek Professional Evaluation If:
  • No progress after 3–4 weeks of consistent daily implementation (minimum 20 requesting opportunities/day)
  • Child shows DECREASING motivation for previously preferred items
  • Child develops NEW challenging behaviours not present before intervention
  • Child shows signs of learned helplessness — stops trying, becomes passive
  • Motor planning difficulties prevent the child from executing ANY requesting response
  • You suspect hearing loss or visual impairment may be affecting communication
🟡 Consult Your Therapy Team If:
  • Progress has plateaued for 2+ weeks despite adaptation attempts
  • Child requests only with one person or in one setting after 6+ weeks
  • Prompt dependency is not resolving despite systematic fading
  • You are feeling overwhelmed, frustrated, or unsupported in implementation

The Big Picture: How Requesting Fits Your Child's Full Development
Requesting is one piece of a larger developmental plan. It directly feeds into five other domains — which is why the Pinnacle GPT-OS® tracks development holistically. No skill exists in isolation.
The 12 developmental domains tracked by GPT-OS®
Functional Communication
Requesting, labeling, commenting
Receptive Language
Following instructions, understanding concepts
Expressive Language
Vocabulary, sentence structure, narrative
Social Interaction
Turn-taking, joint attention, peer play
Cognitive Skills
Problem-solving, cause-effect, memory
Fine Motor Skills
Grip, manipulation, tool use
Gross Motor Skills
Balance, coordination, movement
Sensory Processing
Regulation, tolerance, integration
Self-Care & ADL
Feeding, dressing, hygiene routines
Emotional Regulation
Coping, transitions, frustration tolerance
Play Skills
Symbolic play, imaginative play, structured play
Academic Readiness
Pre-literacy, numeracy, attention to task
Requesting, or manding, directly strengthens several key developmental domains. It supports Functional Communication by giving a child a clear, purposeful way to express needs. It builds Expressive Language by expanding vocabulary and sentence use. It improves Social Interaction through more back-and-forth communication and shared engagement. It supports Cognitive Skills by reinforcing cause-and-effect and problem-solving. And it helps Emotional Regulation by reducing frustration and giving a child a reliable coping tool.
"When a child learns to ask, they don't just gain a skill — they gain agency. And agency changes everything." — Pinnacle Blooms Clinical Team

From Silence to "More Please": Parent Stories
Priya, Mother of Aarav (Age 3, Hyderabad)
"Aarav had zero words at age 2.5. Not one. He would scream and throw himself on the floor when he wanted something. We started with just one button — a recordable device that said 'more please.' The first time he pressed it and I gave him a chip, he looked at me like he'd discovered fire. Within three weeks, he was pressing that button 50 times a day. Now at 3.5, he uses a picture book with 25 items and is starting to say the words. Requesting changed our lives — not just his communication, but our whole family's stress level."
Rajesh, Father of Meera (Age 4, Bangalore)
"We were told Meera would never talk. That was the word — 'never.' We started with signs. MORE. WANT. HELP. Three signs. Within a month, she was signing at the dinner table, at the park, at grandma's house. Last week, she signed WANT while looking at the TV remote, and when I gave it to her, she smiled and signed MORE when her show ended. She may or may not develop speech. But she is communicating. She is asking. She has a voice — it just uses hands instead of words."
Anita, Grandmother of Dev (Age 5, Chennai)
"My daughter-in-law showed me the sign for MORE. I'm 67 years old learning sign language from an app! But when Dev signs MORE CHAPATI to me and I give it to him, and he smiles — that connection is everything. I didn't know I could be part of his therapy. Now I am."
Individual results vary. These stories represent real Pinnacle families (names changed for privacy). Professional assessment is recommended for individualised programming.

The Science: Key Research Behind Teaching Requesting
1
NCAEP Evidence-Based Practices Report (2020)
Manding/requesting training identified as an evidence-based practice with the strongest research support among verbal operant interventions. Based on analysis of 28+ studies meeting rigorous methodological criteria.
2
FCT Meta-Analysis — Tiger, Hanley & Bruzek (2008)
Functional Communication Training reduces challenging behaviour by 80–90% when the communicative alternative is reinforced consistently. Journal of Applied Behaviour Analysis.
3
PECS Efficacy Meta-Analysis — Flippin, Reszka & Watson (2010)
Picture Exchange Communication System demonstrates Level I evidence from multiple RCTs for increasing independent requesting in children with autism.
4
Home-Based Evidence — Padmanabha et al. (Indian J Pediatr, 2019)
Home-based structured interventions delivered by trained caregivers produce significant developmental outcomes in Indian paediatric populations. DOI: 10.1007/s12098-018-2747-4
5
WHO Care for Child Development Package
PMC9978394: Multi-caregiver training is critical for intervention generalisation and maintenance. Parents can be highly effective intervention agents when properly trained and supported.
6
Pinnacle Real-World Evidence
Across 80+ centres, 21 million+ therapy sessions, and 1,000+ clinical professionals: structured manding protocols yield measurable requesting expansion within 4–8 weeks, with 97%+ family-reported improvement.

Consistency Across Caregivers Multiplies Impact — Share This Page
Research shows that multi-caregiver training is critical for generalisation and maintenance of requesting skills. When grandparents, siblings, teachers, and other caregivers all respond consistently to your child's requests, the skill solidifies exponentially faster.
"[Child's name] is learning to ASK for things instead of crying or grabbing. When they show you a picture, make a sign, or press a button — please give them what they're asking for IMMEDIATELY, even if you could just give it to them without the picture, sign, or button. They need to practise, and every time their request WORKS, their brain learns that communication is powerful. Please be patient, enthusiastic, and responsive."

Teacher/School Communication Template: "[Child's name] is currently learning to request using [pictures/signs/a device]. Please ensure the communication system is available at all times and that all requesting attempts are honoured promptly. We are tracking requesting independence — please note any independent requests you observe and share them with the family."
The WHO Care for Child Development Package (PMC9978394) emphasises multi-caregiver training as critical for intervention generalisation and maintenance across environments.

Frequently Asked Questions About Teaching Requesting
Q1: What age should I start teaching requesting?
As early as 12–18 months if your child shows limited requesting behaviours. There is no "too early" for functional communication. If your child is using grabbing, crying, or tantrums to get needs met, they are ready for requesting instruction regardless of age.
Q2: Which modality — speech, signs, pictures, or device?
Start with the modality your child can produce MOST EASILY. For many children, this is picture exchange or a device (lowest motor demand). Signs work well with good imitation skills. Research consistently shows that AAC does NOT prevent speech development — it supports it.
Q3: Will pictures or a device prevent my child from learning to talk?
No. This is the most common myth in communication intervention. Over 30 years of research shows that AAC SUPPORTS speech development. Children who have an effective communication system are MORE likely to develop speech because they understand that communication works.
Q4: How many times a day should we practise?
Structured sessions: 2–3 per day, 10–15 minutes each. Natural opportunities: 20–50+ requesting opportunities throughout daily routines — meals, play, bath, dressing, transitions. The more opportunities, the faster the learning.
Q5: My child can say the word but won't use it to request. Why?
This is the tact/mand distinction in ABA. A child can LABEL "cookie" (tact) but not REQUEST cookie (mand). These are different verbal operants. Create motivation — withhold the labelled item and prompt the requesting form. Reinforce immediately with the cookie.
Q6: My child only requests with me. How do I get generalisation?
Systematically introduce new communication partners. Have them observe first, then practise with your support, then independently. Every new partner gets 3–5 training sessions. Also practise in different settings — requests must work everywhere.
Q7: How long until I see results?
Prompted requesting: days to weeks. Independent requesting: typically 3–6 weeks of consistent practice. Generalised requesting: 6–12 weeks. Every child's timeline differs, but if you are consistent, you WILL see progress.
Q8: What if this technique doesn't work for my child?
No single technique works for every child. If you see no progress after 3–4 weeks of consistent implementation, consult a speech-language pathologist or BCBA for individualised assessment. The Pinnacle Blooms helpline (9100 181 181) can guide you to the right next step.
